Understanding my pathology report

The pathology report is the document that confirms a cancer diagnosis. It is written by a pathologist for other doctors, so it is dense. These are the parts that matter most.

What is in the report

  • Final diagnosisThe most important section, usually near the top. It names the type of cancer and the site. Read this first.
  • Gross descriptionWhat the tissue looked like to the naked eye: size, color, how many pieces. Mostly technical.
  • Microscopic descriptionWhat the pathologist saw under the microscope, and the results of special stains.
  • Addendum or additional reportsResults of extra tests — biomarkers, genetic or molecular tests — may arrive days or weeks later as an addendum or a separate report.

Words you will see

  • Benign / malignant — not cancer / cancer.
  • In situ / invasive — abnormal cells that have stayed in the layer where they started / cells that have grown into surrounding tissue.
  • Grade — how abnormal the cells look and how fast they may grow. Grade is different from stage.
  • Margins — the edges of tissue removed in surgery. Negative or “clear”: no cancer at the edge. Positive: cancer cells reach the edge. Close: cancer is near the edge.
  • Lymph nodes — often written as a fraction, such as “2/15,” meaning 2 of 15 nodes contained cancer.
  • Biomarkers — proteins or gene changes that can guide treatment. For example, breast cancer reports include estrogen receptor (ER), progesterone receptor (PR) and HER2 results.
  • Flow cytometry and cytogenetics — tests used especially for leukemia, lymphoma and myeloma to identify the exact type.

Good to know

  • Reports usually take several days to come back; special tests can take longer.
  • You can ask for a copy. Go over it with your oncologist rather than searching each word alone.
  • A second review of the slides by another pathologist is possible, especially for rare or unclear diagnoses. See second opinions.
